title: Devlens Analysis: The state borrows, households pay the price
excerpt: Bank credit to government grew 36% in a year while lending to business grew 4%, and wages still trail prices. What the squeeze means for NGOs.

image.alt: Shoppers crowd a street market under colourful umbrellas in Motijheel, Dhaka
image.credit: Wasiul Bahar / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

content:
Each week, Devlens looks at the numbers behind the sector. This week we read Bangladesh Bank's latest weekly indicators, published on 15 November, alongside the October price and wage figures from the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) and the government's own budget numbers. Together they describe an economy where the government is taking a growing share of the country's credit, businesses are borrowing little, and households are still losing ground to prices. That matters for anyone running programmes for poor families, and for NGOs that depend on local income.

Where the credit is going

Bangladesh Bank's figures compare September 2026 with September 2025. In that year:

  • Net credit to the government grew by 36.34 percent
  • Credit to the private sector grew by 4.09 percent
  • Total domestic credit grew by 11.18 percent
  • Credit to other public bodies fell by 0.81 percent
  • Broad money (M2) grew by 12.97 percent

The pattern held over the summer. Between June and September 2026, net credit to the government rose 7.46 percent while private credit grew just 0.11 percent. In the twelve months to June 2026, government credit grew 34.52 percent and private credit 4.48 percent.

Put simply, almost all of the growth in lending is going to the state. A private sector that is not borrowing is usually not expanding, and an economy where firms are not expanding is not creating many new jobs. Bangladesh Bank's provisional estimate puts GDP growth at 4.14 percent in 2025-26.

Why the government is borrowing

The government needs the money. The 2026-27 budget sets aside Tk 1,27,520 crore just for interest payments, the finance minister told Parliament on 16 November, with a deficit target of 3.6 percent of GDP. Devlens reported earlier that this interest bill leaves less room for social spending.

At the same time the government is spending little of its development budget. Ministries used only 6.53 percent of the Annual Development Programme in July to October, a record low according to The Business Standard. The two health divisions spent 2.88 and 3.94 percent of their allocations, and Prothom Alo reported that the disaster management ministry had spent 1 percent or less. So the state is borrowing heavily from banks while health clinics, shelters and other public works wait.

The finance minister has also said the government plans a first sovereign bond within two to three months and expects a new IMF agreement by February 2027. Both point to a government looking hard for money, and to more of the budget going on debt.

What households are facing

BBS figures for October show inflation easing slightly, to 8.27 percent from 8.34 percent in September. But the detail is less comforting:

  • Food inflation fell to 6.40 percent, from 7.22 percent
  • Non-food inflation rose to 9.89 percent, from 9.30 percent
  • In rural areas non-food inflation reached 10.21 percent
  • The wage rate index grew 7.63 percent, still below overall inflation

Non-food costs include rent, transport, health care and education. These are the costs that weigh on poor families after they have fed themselves, and they are rising fastest in villages. With wages growing more slowly than prices, the average worker's pay is still buying less each month. Bangladesh Bank's twelve-month average inflation figure is 8.66 percent.

A banking system under strain

The same Bangladesh Bank release shows classified (bad) loans at 32.78 percent of all outstanding loans in June 2026. Net of provisions, the figure is 15.22 percent. Banks with a third of their loan books in trouble are cautious lenders, which helps explain why they prefer to lend to the government.

One bright spot is farm lending. Banks disbursed Tk 10,836.97 crore in agricultural and rural non-farm credit in July to September, up 27.65 percent on a year earlier.

What this means for NGOs

  • More demand, less money. When wages trail prices and jobs are scarce, more families need help with food, health costs and schooling, while the government's own development spending is slow.
  • Cash transfer values lose value. Cash and voucher programmes set months ago now buy less, especially in rural areas where non-food prices are rising fastest. Programme teams may need to review transfer amounts.
  • Microfinance risk. Borrowers whose real incomes are falling find repayments harder, and small businesses that cannot get bank credit lean more on microfinance. NGO lenders will want to watch repayment rates closely.
  • Local fundraising. Corporate giving and local donations tend to fall when businesses are not growing. NGOs trying to replace lost foreign aid with local money face a harder market.
  • Budgets and contracts. NGOs with fixed-price grants or government contracts should check whether staff pay and costs still match what was agreed.

What to watch

BBS's November price figures, due in early December; whether private credit picks up after the IMF talks; the size of the first sovereign bond; and the mid-year revision of the development budget, which will show whether health and disaster spending is cut further.

This analysis is Devlens' own reading of official figures. It does not forecast where the economy is heading, and the numbers will be revised as new data are released.
